content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper investigated the capacities of pre-trained vision-language models in capturing object localization information. It found out normally trained model has limited knowledge of local objects and then the authors proposed a minimum set of modification to enable model's perceptual grouping. Experiments in related tasks such unsupervised segmentation demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This paper is well written and easy to follow.
- The experimental part is relatively comprehensive.

Weaknesses:
- The paper did not propose any new or novel techniques. In detail, the only two modification of CILPpy: employing pretrained weights and adjusting the manner of aggregation across space, do not provide insights to the community.
- Specifically, it is expected that using a strong pretrained model as initialization can improve the performance and there is nothing new about this modification.
- As for the max pooling, it is worthwhile to explore why it works in unsupervised segmentation tasks. It cannot convince me with purely empirical results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written. However, the contributions are not enough to make it published in a top conference due to lack of novelty and more reasonable analysis. Hyperparameters such as learning rate and batch size are not mentioned explicitly, which makes the method hard to reimplement.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is more like a technical report instead of a conference paper. It neither introduces novel ideas nor present some significant empirical results. Only using a more powerful pretrained model as initialization and switching the aggregation function to max pooling are insufficient to be published at a top-tier venue. Thus, I am inclined to reject this paper.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper explores several variants of vision-language models (CLIP) to learn the spatial-aware visual content for the input images. It adopts CLIP as baseline, and takes different initializations of the visual/text encoders, and several feature aggregation strategies.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- The experimental results provide some hints on the model design (for CLIP) to obtain spatial-aware visual cues.
- Achieves good results on zero-shot semantic segmentation.

Cons:
- The main concern for me is the novelty. This paper is more like a technical report rather than a conference paper. It only presents some variants of CLIP designs to obtain spatial-aware visual cues. No further analysis and explanation on why such a design can get better grounding results.
- The exploration is mostly focus on CLIP, not sure whether it can be generalized to other VL pretraining models.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The main concern for me is the novelty, as mentioned previously.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this paper gives some insights on CLIP based representation learning, especially on spatial-aware visual content. However, it's more like a technical report and not satisfied with the qualification of ICLR.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors show that vanilla “vision-language” models do not learn anything about object localization. They then propose a small modifications (different aggregation layer and initialize with pre-training weights) to a current state-of-the-art vision-language model. They show that the modified model, called CLIPpy, achieves good results in unsupervised segmentation and on zero-shot semantic segmentation, as well as learning more robust features (on a simple toy task).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- The paper is well written, clear and easy to follow.
- Moving away from learning global representations of images to learn embeddings that encode local features is a very important problem to the computer vision community. This is the first work (AFAIK) that shows that vision-language models does not perform well on localization (new, but not necessarily very surprising).
- The improvement over the vanilla vision-language model is good, specially given the small modification on the architecture.

### Weaknesses
- The paper has some tones that are prone to hype, such as "The resulting model termed CLIPpy exhibits perceptual grouping" on the end on the Introduction. In my opinion, sentences like that are an over exaggeration and should not be included on the paper (it is not really true and does not add much).
- If I understood well, the “High Quality Image Text Pairs” dataset is not publicly available. Is this the case? This is in itself a red flag IMO, specially because the authors did not mention anything about making it available… If the dataset is indeed not published, why did the authors decide to show results on it? Why not use other available large-scale vision-language data (eg, LAION), so that the work can be reproducible?
- Another weakness of this paper is the lack of novelty. The fact that these vanilla contrastive vision-language models does not learn about object localization (although not shown before) is not particularly surprising. Moreover, initializing the training with pre-trained weights (on either/both vision and language side) is not surprising at all.
- This work is missing a whole corpus of work related to self-supervised learning for local visual features (eg, see [1, 2] for initial works, the papers that cite those initial works, and [3] for a very recent work). These works might achieve competitive/better results without even using any language information. If coupled with language data, they could potentially perform even better. The authors neither mention this line of work, nor compare with any method.
- It is well known that deep learning models (vision, language and vision-language) perform better as more data is available during training (Table 1 corroborates this). Because of that, it would be nice to see SSL models (either that learn global representation, eg DINO, or those models that learn local features) trained on the same amount of images as CLIPpy is trained on (that is, >100M images). 

[1] Unsupervised learning of dense visual representations, Neurips20
[2] Dense Contrastive Learning for Self-Supervised Visual Pre-Training, CVPR21
[3] VICRegL: Self-Supervised Learning of Local Visual Features, arXiv22
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is very clear, well-written, and easy to follow.
- The novelty of the paper is very limited (see above). 
- The paper provide details about the model and training/evaluation protocols. However, the source-code was not provided and it seems the model is trained on private data, which makes reproduction impossible.
content.summary_of_the_review: My initial rating to this paper is 5 (marginally below acceptance rate). Although I believe this direction of work is relevant to the computer vision community, I feel that the novelty (both technical and empirical) is very limited to the scope of this conference.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.details_of_ethics_concerns:
No ethical statement was written.
Even worse, the authors use private data that can have serious biases (and we will never know). They could at least have mentioned something about this.
